USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Maintain current tariff posture and the March 1 deadline as leverage. Do not escalate further, but do not roll back — the US holds a favorable negotiating position as of January 31, 2019. Use the 30 remaining days before the deadline to push for genuine structural concessions from Beijing, not just purchase commitments. Separate the Huawei/DOJ track from trade talks as the administration has publicly done.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The US faces moderate downside risk (threat_score: -0.3), tilted toward opportunity rather than danger. The US economy remains fundamentally sound — Q3 2018 GDP growth was 3.4%, Q4 tracking near 3% (CNBC/Moody's rapid update, Dec 14), consumer confidence stood at 128.1 in December, and the labor market is tight. By contrast, China's economy is in its worst slowdown since 1992 (Politico, Jan 23), with export hubs like Guangdong experiencing 'severe deterioration in foreign orders' (Guardian, Jan 5, citing China Beige Book). Beijing has already blinked on soybeans and auto tariffs ahead of the G20 dinner.

However, the threat is not one-sided. US companies are reporting real pain: Apple cut its sales forecast citing China slowdown magnitude (NPR, Jan 30), and Caterpillar, NVIDIA, Intel, and Harley-Davidson have all cited tariff impacts on earnings. The US goods trade deficit with China hit a record $43.1 billion in October (Business Insider, Jan 9) — undermining the premise that tariffs are reducing the imbalance. The IMF warns a worst-case trade scenario could shave nearly 1% from global GDP, and we are late in the economic cycle. A confidence shock from collapsed talks could tip the US toward recession.

The Huawei indictments (23 counts unsealed Jan 28, including bank fraud, sanctions violations, and trade secret theft from T-Mobile) represent a powerful non-tariff lever. China has limited retaliation options — as the NYT noted (Jan 30), 'Beijing will have few ways to force Washington's hand' given its economic slowdown and eagerness to end the trade war. This is asymmetric leverage in our favor.

The action_score of -0.15 (hold with slight lean toward pressure) reflects the correct posture: the March 1 deadline is our best bargaining chip. Rolling back tariffs prematurely — as Mnuchin has reportedly proposed (Washington Post, Jan 17) — would surrender leverage before structural issues (IP theft, forced tech transfer, state subsidies, market access) are addressed. But further escalation risks a confidence shock to markets that are already jittery after the Q4 selloff (S&P 500 fell 6.24% in 2018). The administration's own internal split — Mnuchin favoring tariff cuts as incentive, Lighthizer and Navarro opposing them — argues for holding firm rather than tilting either way. Lighthizer told Senator Grassley that no progress had been made on structural reform (Politico, Jan 23), which means the tariffs are still working as intended leverage. CSIS expert Scott Kennedy assessed on Jan 23 that 'raising tariffs on March 2nd is the most likely outcome' — this probability itself is leverage.
key_factors: US economy fundamentally strong: Q3 GDP 3.4%, Q4 tracking ~3%, consumer confidence 128.1
China slowdown severe: worst growth since 1992, Guangdong export orders deteriorating sharply
US trade deficit with China hit record $43.1B in October despite tariffs — undermines tariff rationale
Huawei indictments (23 counts, Jan 28) provide asymmetric non-tariff leverage; China has limited retaliation options
Apple, Caterpillar, NVIDIA, Harley-Davidson reporting tariff-related earnings impacts
March 1 deadline (tariffs rise from 10% to 25% on $200B) is primary negotiating leverage
Administration divided: Mnuchin proposes tariff cuts as incentive; Lighthizer/Navarro oppose
No structural progress reported: Lighthizer told Grassley no progress on IP/subsidies/market access
Government shutdown (35 days) just ended, adding domestic political pressure on Trump to show results

sources_cited.excerpt: G20 Buenos Aires dinner: Trump and Xi agree to a 90-day negotiation window. Planned Jan 1, 2019 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% is suspended.
US DOJ unseals fraud and sanctions-related charges against Huawei and Meng; US formally requests Meng's extradition from Canada.
Lighthizer and Mnuchin in Beijing for high-level talks. Purchase commitments discussed; enforcement and structural IP/tech-transfer issues unresolved.
Severe deterioration in foreign orders, especially in the export-sensitive Guangdong region, stands out as a stark example of the pain the tariff war is already causing.
Xi is overseeing a drastic slowdown in China's economic growth... In the last quarter of 2018, China reported the slowest growth rate since its government began publishing quarterly figures in 1992.
Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin in recent weeks has proposed a tariff reduction as an incentive for China to sweeten its offer... Administration hard-liners, including USTR Lighthizer, are opposed.
A 13-count indictment filed in New York City against Huawei, two affiliates and its chief financial officer, Meng Wanzhou, details allegations of bank and wire fraud.
Apple said that they're selling less iPhones in China. Caterpillar said that this was having an impact. NVIDIA, Intel... companies report the effect on their earnings.
The US's trade deficit rose to $55.5 billion in October... China continued to ship significantly more to the US than vice versa, with that deficit reaching a record peak at $43.1 billion.
